senses.learner: to mean to do something that you may well be able to do.
examples: I hope to finish the roof before the rain comes.

senses.learner: a way of behaving that shows no respect for people.
examples: He listened with an air of lazy contempt.

senses.learner: something that has turned out badly
examples: I shall tell Colonel Forster it will be quite a shame if he does not.

connotation.why: names the speaker's regret at the thing rather than a fact about it

senses.learner: the quality of doing what is right and keeping away from what is wrong
examples: It has connected him nearer with virtue than any other feeling.

connotation.why: crediting someone with it approves of them rather than describes them

senses.learner: right conduct in matters of sex
examples: a sister's sense of decency and virtue in such a point should admit of doubt
how little of permanent happiness could belong to a couple who were only brought together because their passions were stronger than their virtue

connotation.why: an approving and indirect name for chastity rather than a plain one

senses.learner: one particular good quality of character
examples: His countenance, voice, and manner, had established him at once in the possession of every virtue.

connotation.why: names the quality as an excellence, so it praises whoever holds it

senses.learner: a polished quality of being graceful and having good taste
examples: Lady Catherine is far from requiring that elegance of dress in us which becomes herself and daughter.
I never saw such capacity, and taste, and application, and elegance, as you describe, united.

connotation.why: calling something elegance approves of its taste rather than reporting it

senses.learner: the quality of a way of solving a problem that is neat and cleverly simple
examples: The elegance of her proof lay in its three short lines.

connotation.why: calling a solution elegant praises it rather than describing its shape

senses.learner: to accept that something is true
examples: He says the delay was the weather's fault, but I don't buy that.

connotation.why: chosen over 'believe' it casts the claim as something being sold
